items.title: NOT IN with a NULL
items.question: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM teams) returns zero rows, even though many users manage nothing. Why?
items.answer: If the subquery returns any NULL, id NOT IN (...) includes the comparison id <> NULL, which is UNKNOWN, so no row can make the predicate TRUE. Use NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery, or filter WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL inside the subquery.

items.title: Three-valued logic
items.body: SQL uses three-valued logic: comparisons involving NULL yield UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows that evaluate to TRUE. So col = NULL never matches; use IS NULL, or IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM for null-safe comparison.

source.name: PostgreSQL docs - Comparison Functions and Operators

items.title: Column order in composite indexes
items.question: Why can an index on (tenant_id, created_at) serve WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at well, but not a query filtering only on created_at?
items.answer: A composite B-tree is sorted by the first column, then by the second within each first-column value, like a phone book sorted by last then first name. Equality on the leading column narrows to one contiguous, already-sorted range. Without it, matching entries are scattered across the whole index.

items.title: 51 queries for one page
items.question: A page lists 50 orders with each customer's name, and the logs show 51 queries. What is the pattern and the fix?
items.answer: The N+1 query pattern: one query for orders, then one per order for its customer, often hidden by lazy-loading ORMs. Fetch with a JOIN, or run one second query with WHERE id IN (...) and stitch results in memory. Per-query round-trip latency usually dominates, not query cost.

items.title: Window functions
items.body: Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) compute across related rows without collapsing them the way GROUP BY does. They turn top-N-per-group and running totals into single queries.

items.title: Isolation levels
items.body: The SQL standard defines isolation levels by which anomalies they permit: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms. Many databases default to READ COMMITTED, where two statements in one transaction can see different committed data.
